name: Central Tarahumara
sweep_summary: cent2131 (Central Tarahumara = Choguita Rarámuri, Guachochi municipality, 'Central' dialect area per Caballero et al. 2022 p. 2) is not in the catalog. All four target items are by Gabriela Caballero and are about word stress in this variety. Read in full: (a) Caballero 2005 ROA-706 manuscript (fetched sources from roa.rutgers.edu, 27 pp.): mixed lexical/default stress system, initial trisyllabic window, no secondary stress, default 2nd-syllable stem stress with weak suffixes and 3rd-syllable with strong suffixes (p. 15); (b) Caballero, Chai & Garellek 2022 OUP chapter (author preprint fetched sources from Yuan Chai's github page): stress lexically contrastive, initial three-syllable window, non-iterative (p. 3), chapter otherwise about tone f0/voice quality and intonation; (c) not in the target list but the authoritative source: Caballero 2022 A grammar of Choguita Rarámuri (LangSci Press, open access; copy already on file in the audit tree), §2.1.2 p. 43 and ch. 5 pp. 133-166. Not obtainable: Caballero 2011 Linguistics (De Gruyter, closed, abstract not retrievable) and Caballero & Carroll 2015 IJAL (closed; abstract saved from Semantic Scholar) — both medium priority only, since the 2022 grammar covers and cites them. The 2008 UC Berkeley dissertation is linked from the author's site only via a login-gated Google Drive link and eScholarship search returned nothing fetchable. Recommended coding for a new catalog record: lexical stress, initial three-syllable window, left-aligned, no secondary stress, deciding source Caballero 2022 grammar p. 43.

new_statements.quote: Stress in Choguita Rarámuri is lexically contrastive and assigned to the first, second or third syllable within an initial three-syllable window. Stress in inflected words is determined by the stress properties of both roots and suffixes: roots are stressed or unstressed (with fixed or shifting stress across paradigms, respectively), while suffixes are stress-shifting or stress-neutral.
new_statements.citation: Caballero, Gabriela (2022). A grammar of Choguita Rarámuri. Comprehensive Grammar Library 5. Berlin: Language Science Press (open access, CC BY). https://langsci-press.org/catalog/book/324
new_statements.locator: §2.1.2 'Stress, tone and prosodic structure', p. 43 (expanded in ch. 5, pp. 133-166; window statement §5.4, p. 161: 'stress in Choguita Rarámuri is restricted to an initial stress window'... 'Choguita Rarámuri stress is clearly left-aligned')
new_statements.reading: Lexical (contrastive) word stress, morphologically conditioned, confined to a left-edge three-syllable window (stress on syllable 1, 2 or 3; never further right). One stress per word, no secondary stress (Caballero 2005 p. 3; Caballero, Chai & Garellek 2022 preprint p. 3). Default for lexically unstressed roots: second syllable of the stem with stress-neutral suffixes, third syllable with stress-shifting suffixes (Caballero 2005 p. 15; grammar Table 2.3 p. 43). Correlates: duration and vowel reduction; a separate three-way lexical tone contrast rides on the stressed syllable. For catalog coding this is a LEXICAL system with an initial three-syllable window (not quantity-sensitive; no contrastive vowel length).

sources.quote: Stress in Choguita Rarámuri is lexically contrastive and assigned to the first, second or third syllable within an initial three-syllable window. Stress in inflected words is determined by the stress properties of both roots and suffixes: roots are stressed or unstressed (with fixed or shifting stress across paradigms, respectively), while suffixes are stress-shifting or stress-neutral.
sources.note: The reference grammar: stress is lexically contrastive (minimal pairs ˈmúri 'basket' / muˈrí 'turtle', ˈéka 'close it!' / eˈká 'wind', p. 134) and assigned to the 1st, 2nd or 3rd syllable within an initial three-syllable window (p. 43, §5.4 p. 161); roots are stressed or unstressed, suffixes stress-shifting or stress-neutral (p. 43, Table 2.3); culminative and obligatory, with duration and vowel reduction as stress correlates, tone (HL/L/H) realized only on the stressed syllable (pp. 133-134); stress is clearly left-aligned and never beyond the third syllable (p. 161-162). No secondary stress…

sources.citation: Caballero, Gabriela, Yuan Chai & Marc Garellek (2022). Stress, tone, and intonation in Choguita Rarámuri. In H. Kubozono, J. Ito & A. Mester (eds), Prosody and Prosodic Interfaces, 227-248. Oxford: OUP.
sources.quote: Stress in CR is lexically contrastive and may exhibit morphologically conditioned shifts. [...] Stress is restricted to appear within an initial-three syllable window on the first, second, or third syllable of the word. There is no evidence for secondary stress assignment; i.e., the system is non-iterative (Caballero 2011). There are no constraints on the alignment of stress with respect to word edges nor any constraints against stress clashes across word boundaries.
sources.note: Chapter is mainly about f0/voice-quality realization of the three lexical tones and tone-intonation interaction, but its background section gives a first-hand statement of the stress system: stress is lexically contrastive (minimal pairs ˈsàwa 'smell' / saˈwá 'leaf', ˈkôt͡ʃi 'pig' / koˈt͡ʃî 'dog'), restricted to an initial three-syllable window, may shift under morphological conditioning, and there is no secondary stress. Confirms Choguita belongs to the 'Central' dialect area (ISO tar), Guachochi municipality (p. 2), i.e. the cent2131 variety.

sources.citation: Caballero Hernández, Gabriela (2005). The stress system of Central Raramuri: Root privilege, prosodic faithfulness and markedness reversals. Ms., University of California, Berkeley. Rutgers Optimality Archive ROA-706 (January 2005), 27 pp.
sources.quote: a) Each prosodic word has a single stress. b) Roots can be accented or unaccented. c) Affixes can be strong or weak [...] d) In words containing no accented roots or strong suffixes, stress falls by default in the second syllable of the stem. e) In words containing an unaccented root and a strong affix, stress falls in the third syllable of the word, the immediately adjacent strong suffix with disyllabic roots, the final root syllable of three-syllable roots. f) Lexical accent in roots blocks default second and third syllable stress. [...] h) There is an initial three-syllable window.
sources.note: First-hand (fieldwork in Choguita, Guachochi, 2003-04, four speakers). A 'mixed' system: lexical accent on roots (632-root database: 1st-syllable stress 12%, 2nd 69%, 3rd 19%, p. 4-5) plus emergent default stress; overarching initial three-syllable window enforced in compounds and multiple affixation; one stress per word, no secondary stress (p. 3); stressed vowels roughly twice as long as unstressed, slightly higher pitch, onset aspiration (p. 3). Default: second syllable of the stem with unaccented roots and weak suffixes, third syllable with strong suffixes (p. 15). Feet analysed as iambic…

sources.quote: we propose that (i) stress-accent and tone are phonologically distinct systems in Choguita Rarámuri; (ii) stress-accent and tone are independent in terms of their acoustic encoding; (iii) both stress-accent and tone are governed in their distribution and makeup by lexical and morphological conditions; (iv) the tone system features a three-way contrast between HL, L, and M; and (v) lexical tonal contrasts are exclusively realized in stressed syllables—that is, tonal distribution is dependent on stress-accent.
